# Files, Directories and Inodes: What a Filesystem Is

Last verified: 2026-10-28 against Linux man-pages (`inode(7)`, `link(2)`, `unlink(2)`, `symlink(7)`, `path_resolution(7)`, `mount(2)`, `mke2fs(8)`, `errno(3)`), docs.kernel.org (VFS, path lookup), the Linux `fs/ext4/ialloc.c` source, Btrfs docs, GNU coreutils (`df`, `stat`), macOS `df(1)`, OSTEP chapters 39 and 40, and re-runs of Demos 1 to 4 on macOS. Linux commands are not run here.

Starts from: "Programs, Processes and the Kernel" (system calls, file descriptors) and "How a Computer Runs Code" (RAM versus disk). Nothing else.

## The problem and why it matters

Storage failures arrive as short sentences: "No space left on device" while `df` shows free space; "I deleted the huge log and the disk is still full"; "Permission denied" on a file whose mode looks fine; "Cross-device link". Each names a rule of the filesystem; this lesson builds that model.

A disk (or SSD) only stores numbered chunks called *blocks*; it knows nothing of names, owners or folders. A *filesystem* is the data layout plus the kernel code that turns those blocks into files, directories and permissions.

## First principles

1. **A file is bytes plus metadata.** The kernel does not know whether the bytes are a photo or source code; the filesystem's job is to store them persistently and give them back unchanged. *Metadata* means data about the data: owner, size, timestamps.
2. **Metadata lives in an *inode*** (index node): a small record per file. `inode(7)`: "Each file has an inode containing metadata about the file." It holds the owner, permission bits, size, timestamps, a *link count*, and where the data blocks are (OSTEP). It does **not** hold the file's name.
3. **An inode number identifies the file inside one filesystem.** `inode(7)`: numbers are "guaranteed to be unique only within a filesystem".
4. **A directory is a file whose contents are a list of (name, inode number) pairs.** OSTEP: it "contains a list of (user-readable name, low-level name) pairs". So the name belongs to the *directory*, not the file. Renaming edits an entry; the data does not move.
5. **One inode can have many names.** A *hard link* is another directory entry pointing at the same inode. `link(2)`: afterwards "it is impossible to tell which name was the original". The inode's link count says how many names it has.
6. **`rm` removes a name, not necessarily the file.** `unlink(2)` "deletes a name from the filesystem"; the file is deleted when the last name is gone *and* no process holds it open. If one does, it persists "until the last file descriptor referring to it is closed".
7. **A symbolic link (symlink) is a tiny file whose contents are a path.** `symlink(7)`: "a pointer to another name, and not to an underlying object". It can dangle, meaning the path points at nothing.
8. **Permissions are nine bits** in the inode: read, write, execute for owner, group and everyone else (`inode(7)`: "the least significant 9 bits (0777)"). On a directory, execute means *search*: without it you cannot look names up (`path_resolution(7)`: "If the process does not have search permission on the current lookup directory, an EACCES error is returned").
9. **Many filesystems share one tree through mounting.** `mount(2)`: "attaches the filesystem specified by source ... to the location (a directory or file) specified by the pathname in target"; that directory is the *mount point*. Inode numbers and hard links stop at the boundary.
10. **Two separate budgets: space and inodes.** On filesystems that fix the inode count when they are made (ext2/3/4, see the failure scenario below), you can run out of inodes while blocks are free. Others (Btrfs lists "Dynamic inode allocation") do not have that failure in the same form.

## How it works

### Names, inodes and data

```
 directory /data          inode table
 +--------+-------+
 | a.txt  |  117 -------> inode 117
 | b.txt  |  117 -------> links: 2, size: 6
 | s.txt  |  120 --+      owner, mode, block list
 +--------+-------+ |            |
                    |            v
                    |        "hello"  (data block)
                    |
                    +----> inode 120 (a symlink)
                           its data is the text "a.txt"
```

Two names, one inode (a hard link). `s.txt` is a different inode whose data is the text `a.txt`; it follows a path, not an inode.

### What `open` and `read` do

```
 open("/var/log/app.log")
   |
   v  start at root directory "/"
   +--> look up "var" in /     -> inode of var
   +--> look up "log" in var   -> inode of log
   +--> look up "app.log"      -> inode of app.log
   |      (each step needs search permission)
   v
 kernel makes an open-file object that points at the inode
 and returns fd 3 (the lowest free descriptor)
   |
 read(3, buf, n) --> inode says which blocks hold the bytes
                 --> page cache first, disk if missing
```

This fills in the last box of the descriptor table from the previous lesson. The Linux kernel keeps recently used name-to-inode lookups in RAM; its docs call them *dentries* (directory entries) and say they "live in RAM and are never saved to disc".

### Demo 1: two names, one inode, and a symlink

```bash
echo "hello" > a.txt && ln a.txt b.txt && ln -s a.txt s.txt
ls -li
stat -f 'name=%N inode=%i links=%l size=%z' a.txt b.txt s.txt
rm a.txt; ls -li; cat b.txt; cat s.txt
```

Captured here on macOS (the `--- after rm ---` divider is my annotation, the `total` lines are trimmed, `@` after the mode means extended attributes on macOS, and inode numbers will differ per run). On Linux `stat -f` means something else (it reports the filesystem, per the GNU coreutils manual); use `stat -c '%n %i %h %s'` (name, inode, links, size), not run here:

```text
64152317 -rw-r--r--@ 2 ryanhamby  wheel  6 Oct 28 18:53 a.txt
64152317 -rw-r--r--@ 2 ryanhamby  wheel  6 Oct 28 18:53 b.txt
64152320 lrwxr-xr-x@ 1 ryanhamby  wheel  5 Oct 28 18:53 s.txt -> a.txt
name=a.txt inode=64152317 links=2 size=6
name=b.txt inode=64152317 links=2 size=6
name=s.txt inode=64152320 links=1 size=5
--- after rm a.txt ---
64152317 -rw-r--r--@ 1 ryanhamby  wheel  6 Oct 28 18:53 b.txt
64152320 lrwxr-xr-x@ 1 ryanhamby  wheel  5 Oct 28 18:53 s.txt -> a.txt
hello
cat: s.txt: No such file or directory
```

The first column of `ls -li` is the inode number: `a.txt` and `b.txt` share one and show a link count of 2. After `rm a.txt` the data survives under `b.txt` (count 1), but the symlink now dangles. The symlink's size, 5, is the length of the text `a.txt`: its "data" is the path.

### Demo 2: a descriptor keeps an unlinked file alive

```python
import os, tempfile
d = tempfile.mkdtemp(); path = os.path.join(d, "notes.txt")
open(path, "w").write("hello")
fd = os.open(path, os.O_RDONLY)
print("same inode as the path?", os.fstat(fd).st_ino == os.stat(path).st_ino)
os.unlink(path)                       # remove the name
print("names in directory:", os.listdir(d))
print("read via fd:", os.read(fd, 100), "| links:", os.fstat(fd).st_nlink)
```

```text
same inode as the path? True
names in directory: []
read via fd: b'hello' | links: 0
```

No name, link count 0, yet the data is still readable. Closing `fd` is what lets the kernel free it.

### Demo 3: permissions and directory search

```bash
echo secret > f.txt; chmod 000 f.txt; cat f.txt
mkdir sub; echo x > sub/g.txt; chmod 600 sub; cat sub/g.txt
```

```text
cat: f.txt: Permission denied
cat: sub/g.txt: Permission denied
```

The second failure is the surprise: `g.txt` has the default mode (readable), but its directory `sub` lacked execute (search), so the path could not be walked.

### Demo 4: a mount boundary

I made an 8 MiB disk image, mounted it at `/Volumes/drilltest` (`mount` listed it as `hfs, local, nodev, nosuid, journaled, ...`), and tried a hard link across:

```text
ln: /Volumes/drilltest/c.txt: Cross-device link
```

`stat -f dev=%d` printed different device numbers for the two directories. `link(2)` documents this as `EXDEV`: the paths "are not on the same mounted filesystem" (Linux words the message "Invalid cross-device link", per `errno(3)`). A symlink worked: I created one on the image pointing at a file outside it, and `cat` read through it; `symlink(7)` says symlinks "may cross filesystem boundaries".

Last: `df -i` on Linux (GNU coreutils) will "List inode usage information instead of block usage"; macOS `df -i` "Include[s] statistics on the number of free and used inodes". On that macOS volume it reported about 4.29 billion free inodes. Whether a filesystem has a fixed inode count depends on its design; the exhaustion failure was not run here, but the ext4 allocator source (`fs/ext4/ialloc.c`, `__ext4_new_inode`) sets `err = -ENOSPC` when no block group has a free inode.

## Worked failure scenario

**Symptom:** a batch job fails with `No space left on device` (`ENOSPC`), yet `df -h` shows 40 percent free (hypothetical figure).

1. **Check inodes, not just bytes.** `df -i` on the mount. If inode use is near 100 percent, the filesystem has no free inode to name a new file, so creation fails even with free blocks.
2. **Find the swarm.** Millions of tiny files (cache entries, one file per request) each use one inode. Count files per directory with `find` (not run here).
3. **Why it is not a setting to flip.** `mke2fs(8)`: "mke2fs creates an inode for every bytes-per-inode bytes of space on the disk", and "it is not possible to change this ratio on a file system after it is created" (resizing keeps the ratio, so a bigger volume gets proportionally more inodes). Other filesystems, such as Btrfs, allocate inodes dynamically; check yours.
4. **If instead `df` says full after deleting:** a process still holds a deleted file open. The next lesson reproduces this and shows the `lsof` check.

**Fix:** delete or pack the small files into one file or a database; alert on inode use as well as bytes; for a new volume holding many small files, choose its filesystem and inode ratio for that.

## Tradeoffs

| Use when | Avoid when |
|---|---|
| Hard link: two names for one file on the same filesystem, instant "copy" with no extra space | The names must survive on different mounts; a link cannot cross them |
| Symlink: point at a path, cross mounts, swap targets for "current release" style pointers (create a new link, then `rename` it over the old one, since `rename` replaces atomically) | You need the data to survive removal of the original path; the link will dangle |
| Many small files: simple code, easy to inspect | Millions of them: each costs an inode and a directory entry |

## Interview questions

1. What is an inode? Where is the file's name stored? *Probe:* what does a directory contain? *Outline:* metadata record; name is in the directory entry (name to inode number); the inode has a link count.
2. What happens on `rm`? *Outline:* unlink removes one name; data lives until the count is 0 and no descriptor is open.
3. Hard link versus symlink? *Outline:* same inode versus a file holding a path; hard links stay on one filesystem and not for directories; symlinks can dangle and can cross mounts.
4. A file shows mode `644` yet `open` fails with permission denied. Why? *Outline:* a directory on the path lacks search permission, or the process runs as another user; check every component.
5. `df` shows free space but writes fail. *Outline:* inode exhaustion (`df -i`), a quota, or a read-only mount; check each.
6. Walk me through `open("/var/log/app.log")`. *Outline:* the lookup diagram, then a descriptor pointing at an open-file object and the inode.

**Whiteboard exercise:** draw a directory with two names for one file and a symlink to it, with the link count. `rm` the first name, then the second, while a process holds the file open; at each step say what exists and is readable.

## Checklist

1. I can say what is in an inode and what a directory contains.
2. I can predict link counts after `ln`, `ln -s` and `rm`.
3. I can explain why an open file survives `rm`.
4. I can name two ways "No space left on device" happens with free bytes.
5. I ran the `ls -li` and unlink-while-open demos.

## Common wrong answers

- "The file name is stored in the file." It is in the directory.
- "`rm` erases the data." It removes a name; data stays while another name or a descriptor remains.
- "A hard link is a copy." No extra data; both names are the file.
- "Read permission on the file is enough." Every directory on the path needs search permission.
- "Out of space always means out of bytes." Inodes are a second budget.

## Sources

Checked 2026-10-28 (fetched and read):
- man7.org `inode(7)`: inode as metadata, inode numbers "unique only within a filesystem", nine permission bits (0777), `st_nlink`. `link(2)`: "impossible to tell which name was the original", `EXDEV` ("not on the same mounted filesystem"), `EPERM` when `oldpath` is a directory. `symlink(7)`: path contents, dangling, "may cross filesystem boundaries". `unlink(2)`: "deletes a name from the filesystem", file persists until the last descriptor is closed. `mount(2)`: attaches a filesystem at a directory. `path_resolution(7)`: search permission and `EACCES`. `mke2fs(8)`: bytes-per-inode, fixed after creation, resizing keeps the ratio. `errno(3)`: `EXDEV` and `ENOSPC` messages.
- docs.kernel.org VFS page: an inode represents "an object within the filesystem"; "A single inode can be pointed to by multiple dentries"; dentries "live in RAM and are never saved to disc". Linux `fs/ext4/ialloc.c`: `-ENOSPC` when no group has a free inode.
- GNU coreutils manual: `df --inodes`, `stat -f` (filesystem status), `stat -c` sequences `%n %i %h %s`. macOS `df(1)` man page: `-i`. Btrfs docs: "Dynamic inode allocation".
- OSTEP chapters 39 (Files and Directories: directory as (user-readable name, low-level name) pairs; hard links, reference count, symbolic links, mounting) and 40 (File System Implementation: inode contents, inode bitmap and a fixed 80-inode table in the toy filesystem).
- Demos 1 to 4 re-run on one Apple M4 Mac (macOS); the test image was detached afterwards.

Not run or checked: every Linux command (`stat -c`, `find`, `df -i` on ext4); inode exhaustion itself (the allocator source was read, not exercised); whether APFS or XFS allocate inodes on demand.
